item.title: Entrepreneurship Ex Machina: Transformative AI for Theory and Practice
item.content:encoded:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally reshaping entrepreneurship and the broader entrepreneurial ecosystem. From AI-powered ideation and opportunity recognition to automated scaling and intelligent resource allocation, AI technologies are transforming how entrepreneurs identify opportunities, make decisions, and execute their ventures. This special issue seeks to advance our understanding of how AI is reshaping entrepreneurial theory and practice, and to explore both the opportunities and challenges that emerge from this transformation.

We invite submissions that explore the intersection of AI and entrepreneurship across multiple dimensions. This includes understanding how entrepreneurs leverage AI tools and platforms, how AI influences venture funding and investment decisions, how AI enables new business models and competitive advantages, and how AI impacts entrepreneurial ecosystems and the broader economy. We are particularly interested in work that examines both the promise and pitfalls of AI adoption in entrepreneurial contexts.

The special issue welcomes empirical studies, theoretical contributions, methodological innovations, and practitioner perspectives that shed light on AI's role in entrepreneurship. Submissions may examine startups, established companies pursuing entrepreneurial initiatives, or the broader institutional and infrastructural changes enabled by AI. We encourage interdisciplinary approaches that integrate insights from entrepreneurship, artificial intelligence, management, economics, and related fields.

Potential topics

  • AI's transformative impact on entrepreneurial ecosystems
  • Machine learning applications in startup scaling and growth
  • Algorithmic decision-making in venture capital and funding allocation
  • AI-driven business model innovation and experimentation
  • Automation and augmentation of entrepreneurial tasks
  • Ethical implications and responsible AI use in entrepreneurship
  • AI's role in identifying and exploiting market opportunities
  • Digital transformation of entrepreneurial processes
  • Human-AI collaboration in entrepreneurial ventures
  • Generative AI and creative entrepreneurship
  • Data analytics for entrepreneurial decision-making
  • AI-enabled new venture creation and ideation

item.title: Enhancing Transparency and Replicability in Entrepreneurship Research with Preregistrations, Registered Reports, and Registered Revisions
item.content:encoded:
Entrepreneurship research, like many social sciences, faces challenges related to publication bias, selective reporting, and limited replicability of findings. While transparency and open science initiatives have gained traction in psychology and other fields, entrepreneurship research has been slower to adopt preregistration and registered reports. This special issue seeks to advance entrepreneurship scholarship by promoting transparency, replicability, and rigorous methodology through preregistration, registered reports, and registered revisions.

We welcome submissions that demonstrate how preregistration, registered reports, and registered revisions can enhance entrepreneurship research quality. Studies using these methods to examine key entrepreneurship questions, as well as methodological papers discussing implementation challenges, best practices, and frameworks for adoption within the entrepreneurship community, are encouraged.

Potential topics

  • Preregistration of studies
  • Registered reports as a publication format
  • Registered revisions to address reviewer comments
  • Transparency in entrepreneurship research methodology
  • Replication studies in entrepreneurship
  • Open science practices in entrepreneurship
  • Research design and analysis plans
  • Managing researcher degrees of freedom
  • Reducing publication bias in entrepreneurship research
  • Challenges and best practices for implementing transparency methods

item.title: The Startup Workforce
item.content:encoded:
Edited for Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice, .

Startups operate in unique organizational contexts characterized by resource constraints, rapid growth, uncertainty, and dynamic change. These distinctive features shape how startups attract, develop, and retain talent, creating workforce challenges and opportunities that differ significantly from established organizations.

The startup workforce represents a critical yet understudied area of organizational research. While entrepreneurship literature has traditionally focused on founders and venture capital, the employees who join startups and contribute to their success deserve greater scholarly attention. Understanding startup employment practices, workforce composition, and employee experiences provides important insights into contemporary work arrangements and organizational dynamics.

This special issue seeks papers that examine all aspects of the startup workforce, including recruitment strategies, retention mechanisms, organizational culture, compensation approaches, employee well-being, team dynamics, diversity considerations, and the experiences of workers in early-stage ventures. We welcome empirical studies, theoretical contributions, and practical insights that advance our knowledge of how startups build and manage their human capital.

Research on startup workforces has implications for multiple stakeholder groups including startup founders and managers seeking to build effective teams, employees considering careers in startups, policymakers designing support for entrepreneurial ecosystems, and scholars interested in organizational behavior and human resource management in non-traditional contexts.

Potential topics

  • Hiring and recruitment in startups
  • Employee retention and turnover in startups
  • Compensation and benefits in startup environments
  • Organizational culture and dynamics in early-stage companies
  • Leadership and management styles in startups
  • Skills development and training in startups
  • Diversity and inclusion in startup workforces
  • Remote work and distributed teams in startups
  • Employee motivation and engagement in startups
  • Career trajectories and job transitions in startup contexts
  • Human resource practices and policies in startups
  • Entrepreneurial teams and co-founder dynamics

item.title: Time in Entrepreneurship: New Perspectives and Approaches
item.content:encoded:
Katrin B. Hussinger, University of Luxembourg

Philipp Zahn, Lund University

Entrepreneurship is inherently a temporal phenomenon. Entrepreneurs navigate through time as they create and develop new ventures, make critical decisions under uncertainty, and manage the tensions between short-term pressures and long-term vision. Despite the pervasive role of time in entrepreneurial processes, entrepreneurship scholarship has largely overlooked temporal dimensions in favor of static, cross-sectional analyses. This special issue aims to address this gap by bringing together research that explicitly examines time-related aspects of entrepreneurship.

We seek papers that advance our understanding of how time shapes entrepreneurial activities and outcomes. This includes research on temporal dimensions of opportunity recognition, the timing of resource acquisition, the speed of venture development, temporal aspects of team dynamics, historical perspectives on entrepreneurial ventures, and how entrepreneurs' time orientation influences strategic choices. We also welcome studies that employ temporal methodologies such as longitudinal designs, event history analysis, and qualitative process studies.

Papers should make meaningful theoretical or empirical contributions to our understanding of time in entrepreneurship. We encourage interdisciplinary approaches that draw on insights from psychology, sociology, economics, and management studies. Research examining time across different contexts—geographic, sectoral, and institutional—is particularly welcome.

Potential topics

  • Temporal dimensions of entrepreneurial processes
  • Time perception and decision-making in entrepreneurship
  • Temporal aspects of opportunity recognition and exploitation
  • Speed of venture creation and growth
  • Long-term orientation and sustainability in entrepreneurial ventures
  • Timing and market entry strategies
  • Temporal patterns in entrepreneurial ecosystems
  • Historical and longitudinal perspectives on entrepreneurship
  • Temporal heterogeneity among entrepreneurs
  • Time management and work-life balance in entrepreneurship
  • Rhythms and cycles in entrepreneurial activities
  • Future orientation and strategic planning in new ventures

item.title: Reexamining and Replicating Foundational Studies in Entrepreneurship Research
item.content:encoded:
James O. Fiet, ,

Per Davidsson,

Entrepreneurship research has accumulated a substantial body of foundational work over the past several decades. These seminal studies have shaped our understanding of entrepreneurial processes, behaviors, and outcomes. However, the field would benefit from systematic efforts to reexamine and replicate these foundational studies to assess their robustness, generalizability, and continued relevance.

This special issue invites submissions that directly engage with foundational entrepreneurship research through replication, reexamination, and extension. We seek studies that either directly replicate foundational work, conduct conceptual replications in new contexts, perform meta-analyses of key findings, or critically reexamine the theoretical foundations of influential entrepreneurship research.

Such work is crucial for establishing the credibility and reliability of our knowledge base, identifying boundary conditions for existing theories, and determining which foundational findings hold across diverse contexts and populations. This special issue aims to strengthen entrepreneurship research by promoting transparency, reproducibility, and critical evaluation of our most influential work.

Potential topics

  • Replication studies of foundational entrepreneurship research
  • Conceptual replications that extend foundational work in new contexts or with new populations
  • Direct replications of seminal empirical studies
  • Meta-analyses of foundational entrepreneurship research
  • Critiques and reexaminations of influential theories and models in entrepreneurship
  • Studies that challenge or refine existing entrepreneurship frameworks
  • Investigations into the generalizability of foundational entrepreneurship findings across cultures, time periods, and industries

item.title: The Startup Workforce
item.content:encoded:
This special issue aims to explore the multifaceted dimensions of workforce dynamics, human resource management, and employment relationships within startup organizations. Startups present unique organizational contexts that differ significantly from established corporations in terms of resource constraints, growth trajectories, organizational structures, and employment practices.

Potential topics

  • Employment relationships in startups
  • Work organization and management practices in startup contexts
  • Workforce diversity and inclusion in startups
  • Entrepreneurship and human resource management
  • Employee motivation and retention in startups
  • Organizational culture in startup environments
  • Skills development and training in startups
  • Labor market dynamics and startup employment
  • Remote work and flexible arrangements in startups
  • Founder-employee relationships
  • Work-life balance in startup settings
